compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the seed's multi-file/Blueprint architecture for a single-file monolith, forcing Session 4 to pay the cost of re-extracting a repository layer
requirements.txt was never maintained holistically — the final file lists only Flask-Limiter and redis, omitting Flask, PyJWT, Celery, and Werkzeug which the app imports
Session 4's update_task reconstructs column names from SQL fragments (field.split(' = ')[0]) in the HTTP layer, a fragile coupling between app.py and repository semantics
Session 5 pagination computes total by loading all owner rows (len(list(...))) on every request, O(n) work per page that compounds at scale
key_decisions: Session 1: full greenfield rewrite of the seed into a minimal single-file CRUD API, discarding the Blueprint/roles/tokens scaffolding
Session 2: JWT bearer auth (PyJWT HS256) with per-user ownership scoping on every query plus non-destructive ALTER TABLE migrations
Session 3: Celery/Redis background queue for task-completion notifications, adding an external-infra dependency and a users.email field
Session 4: extraction of a BaseRepository ABC with UserRepository/TaskRepository to move all raw SQL out of the Flask layer
Session 5: user-scoped rate limiting (Flask-Limiter) and keyset cursor pagination with a breaking response-envelope change
Session 3→5 kept schema changes migration-safe (CREATE IF NOT EXISTS + PRAGMA-driven ALTER TABLE), never dropping rows
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean but deliberately minimal monolith, discarding the seed's modularity; Session 2 layered in well-scoped authentication with solid ownership isolation on every query and migration-safe schema changes; Session 3 added async notifications as a reasonable small integration; Session 4 was a strong refactor that consolidated all SQL into a repository layer; Session 5 capped the arc with real production concerns — rate limiting and cursor pagination — backed by thorough tests. The only persistent warts are the fragile column-name reconstruction in update_task, an under-maintained requirements.txt, and O(n) total-count pagination, but the arc is unambiguously one of increasing structure, test coverage (17 passing), and production readiness.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session progression from a bare task API to a production-flavored multi-user service with auth, ownership isolation, async notifications, a repository layer, rate limiting, and pagination — quality rising with each session despite minor long-lived warts like an incomplete requirements.txt and a fragile SQL-field reconstruction in the update path.
